summary: George Cameron, co-founder and CPO of Artificial Analysis, introduces the company as a leading independent AI benchmarking platform benchmarking over 150 models across modalities including language, vision, speech, image generation, and video generation, with most results published free on their website. Their intelligence index is a composite of seven evaluations providing a generalist perspective on model intelligence. Cameron frames the AI landscape since ChatGPT's launch, noting the rapid acceleration of model releases. The current intelligence leaderboard shows O3 leading, followed by o4-mini high, DeepSeek R1, Rock 3 mini reasoning high, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Claude 4 Opus thinking. He emphasizes there are multiple frontiers in AI beyond raw intelligence, each with trade-offs. The reasoning models frontier reveals an order of magnitude difference in output tokens between reasoning and non-reasoning models. GPT 4.1 required 7 million tokens to run the intelligence index, while o4-mini high required 72 million and Gemini 2.5 Pro required 130 million. This verbosity translates to latency: GPT 4.1 took 4.7 seconds median response time versus over 40 seconds for o4-mini high. The open weights frontier shows the gap to proprietary models has closed significantly, with DeepSeek V3 and R1 within a couple points of leading proprietary models. Chinese labs including DeepSeek and Alibaba with Qwen 3 lead open weights. The cost frontier shows GPT-4 level intelligence costs fallen over 100x since mid-2023. O3 cost $2,000 to run the intelligence index while GPT 4.1 nano is over 500x cheaper. The speed frontier shows output speed increasing from approximately 40 tokens per second in 2023 to over 300 tokens per second for equivalent intelligence, driven by MoE sparsity, distillation, software optimizations like flash attention and speculative decoding, and hardware improvements with B200 achieving over 1,000 tokens per second. Cameron concludes with the future of compute demand: despite efficiency gains, compute demand will continue increasing due to larger models (DeepSeek has over 600 billion total parameters), insatiable demand for more intelligence, reasoning models requiring more inference compute, and agents making 20 to 100+ sequential requests that multiply compute demand.

takeaways: There are multiple AI frontiers beyond raw intelligence—reasoning, open weights, cost, and speed—each with important trade-offs for application builders

sections.title: Introduction to Artificial Analysis
sections.summary: George Cameron introduces Artificial Analysis as an independent AI benchmarking company covering intelligence, speed, cost, hardware, and multiple modalities (language, vision, speech, image, video) for over 150 models, with most data published free on their website.

sections.title: State of AI Progress
sections.summary: Overview of rapid AI progress since ChatGPT launch. Current intelligence leaderboard shows O3 leading, followed by o4-mini high, DeepSeek R1, Rock 3 mini reasoning high, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Claude 4 Opus thinking. Introduces the concept of multiple frontiers beyond raw intelligence.

sections.title: The Reasoning Models Frontier
sections.summary: Explores trade-offs of reasoning models: order of magnitude more output tokens (GPT 4.1: 7M vs o4-mini high: 72M vs Gemini 2.5 Pro: 130M), 10x latency increase (4.7s vs 40s+), and implications for agentic applications where 30 sequential queries can mean 5 minutes versus 30 seconds of wait time.

sections.title: The Open Weights Frontier
sections.summary: The intelligence gap between open weights and proprietary models has closed significantly. DeepSeek V3 and R1 brought open weights within a couple points of leading proprietary models. Chinese labs (DeepSeek, Alibaba Qwen 3) lead open weights, with Meta and Nvidia following.

sections.title: The Cost Frontier
sections.summary: GPT-4 level intelligence costs have fallen over 100x since mid-2023. O3 cost $2,000 to run intelligence index while GPT 4.1 nano is 500x cheaper. Emphasizes total cost including reasoning token verbosity, not just per-token pricing. Cost structures that do not work today may become feasible in 6 months.

sections.title: The Speed Frontier
sections.summary: Output speed increased from ~40 to over 300 tokens/second for equivalent intelligence, driven by MoE sparsity, distillation, software optimizations (flash attention, speculative decoding), and hardware improvements (B200: 1,000+ tokens/second). Cameron notes specialized accelerators like Cerebras, Samova, and Grock.

sections.title: The Future of Compute Demand
sections.summary: Cameron concludes that despite efficiency gains, compute demand will continue to increase. Key drivers include larger models (DeepSeek over 600 billion total parameters), insatiable demand for more intelligence, reasoning models requiring more inference compute, and agents making 20 to 100+ sequential requests that multiply compute demand.
